description: **Assembly deploys are a command, not embedded CI shell.** `selfblog assembly integrate` performs the whole deploy body -- version detection, subtree replacement, artifact filtering, membership bookkeeping, the push retry loop and search indexing -- and the generated workflow is six thin steps that invoke it. `selfblog assembly sync-workflow` regenerates the deployed workflow on every release and pins the selfblog version it installs, so it can no longer drift from the generator. The Git Data API push path now carries binary content, skips files whose bytes already match the remote, and can delete paths. `assembly push` resolves the tag that names the version being dispatched instead of the repository's newest tag, and refuses to dispatch a version missing from selfdoc.json's versions.

**Unified site pages address their own mount.** Constituent projects on a unified site mount at `<locale>/<slug>/<version>`, and page addressing now carries the project segment, so asset links, canonicals and hreflang on a unified page resolve to real files instead of paths one or two levels short.

**`selfblog check` honors the configured coverage threshold.** The unified path demanded that every public symbol be documented regardless of `coverage_threshold`, so a project that lowered the threshold passed `selfdoc check` and failed `selfblog check` on identical state. Both entry points now reach the same verdict.

**Post checks no longer need the selfdoc package.** `check_posts` reads POST001-POST005 severities from the lint registry in selfdoc-core instead of importing `selfdoc.check`, so a posts-only install runs them with selfblog alone.
**`parse_post` is public.** Post validation, slug derivation and metadata now live in one function that works on any markdown source, not just a file on disk.

**An assembly dispatch must name the version the build will actually produce.** `assembly push` accepted any version present in `selfdoc.json`'s `versions`, so dispatching an older one published the newest version's docs recorded under the older version's name. The dispatched version now has to be the newest declared one, and the refusal names both. A blank newest `versions` entry -- previously refused only when a second entry existed, and otherwise built unversioned at the wrong address -- is a hard error however long the array is.

**An assembly rebuild refuses an incomplete membership record.** `assembly rebuild` turned a missing version into the literal string `latest`, which travelled through the dispatch payload and back into the assembly's own `projects.json`. A record missing `repo`, `ref` or `version` is now a hard error naming the project and the missing fields.

**The generated deploy workflow pins every tool it installs.** selfdoc and pagefind floated on the same install line that pinned selfblog, so a released change to either could break every project's deploy at once -- the exact failure the selfblog pin exists to prevent. All three are pinned now and rewritten on every `assembly sync-workflow` run, with `--pin-selfdoc` and `--pin-pagefind` to name them explicitly.

**`assembly sync-workflow` refuses a pin PyPI cannot serve.** The selfblog pin defaults to the running selfblog, which in a checkout is an editable install ahead of the registry, so the written workflow could carry a `pip install selfblog==X` that resolves nowhere -- surfacing later as a failed deploy on the assembly repository. Every pin is now checked against PyPI before anything is written, and an unpublished one aborts the run naming the version and the registry.

**The unified landing page's links resolve.** The projects page at `<locale>/common/<version>/projects/` asked for `../style.css` (the stylesheet is at the site root) and gave each project card a site-root path with no relative hop, so neither the styling nor any card worked. Both now come from the landing page's own address.

**`selfblog check --ignore` refuses a code the lint registry does not carry.** A mistyped code silently suppressed nothing; the flag is validated against the registry before any check work runs, and an unknown code aborts naming the known codes.

**A release no longer destroys documentation published between releases.** A full build replaced the project's whole section in the assembly, so a post or a documentation update published since the last release died at the next one. Each publisher now records the files it produced and removes only the ones it produced before and no longer produces -- a page the build dropped still disappears, everything else stays. Assembly membership moved to a hand-edited `roster.toml` in the assembly repository that every deploy reconciles to: a project that leaves the roster loses its section, its manifests, its membership record and its search-index entries, and a dispatch can no longer add a project by arriving. The file is required, and a deploy without it stops with instructions.

**Two new ways to change what the assembly serves, neither of which needs a release.** `selfblog docs publish` is the documentation counterpart of `post publish`: it builds locally and pushes the project's section, its manifest and its membership entry into the assembly repository in one commit, images and all, deleting the pages the project no longer builds as it goes, then dispatches a rebuild of the shared elements. `selfblog assembly retire --slug <slug>` does the opposite and was previously impossible without hand-editing the assembly: it removes the project from the roster and deletes its whole section and every one of its manifests in one commit, so the listing, feed, sitemap and search index stop naming it. Both are consequential.

**The unified site follows the new addressing scheme, and every project's posts land in one `blog/` tree.** Each constituent mounts its current version at `<slug>/` and its superseded versions at `<slug>/v/<version>/`; the locale segment is gone while there is one locale. Posts are site-level: whichever project wrote one, it is emitted at `blog/<slug>/`, so a slug repeated across projects is a hard error naming both.

**A post slug repeated across two projects is refused when the assembly merges them, naming both.** Posts share one slug namespace across the assembled site, but each project's posts arrive as its own manifest, so no single build ever saw two projects' posts together: the blog index, the feed and the sitemap silently disagreed. All three now merge through one function that refuses the collision, and the assembly has one address authority those generators, the cross-project link check and the deploy-time verification all read.

**The assembled site is verified before the deploy pushes it, and `selfblog assembly verify` runs the same assertions by hand.** One read-only pass over the built tree checks that the roster, the subtrees and the manifests name the same projects, that every page and post a manifest lists was emitted, that the shared artifacts exist and parse, that every internal reference, sitemap entry, feed link and cross-project link resolves, that every page has a title and a canonical under the site's base, and that no unresolved directive or per-project routing file survived. A broken tree now fails with nothing deployed. The assembly also writes its own `robots.txt` and root 404, which previously ended up buried under each project's prefix.

**Posts are served at `/blog/<post-slug>/`, at the site level, and the deploy publishes them there.** The graft copied a project's whole build into its own subtree, so a post landed at `/<slug>/blog/<post>/`; the blog index linked `/<slug>/posts/<post>/`; and the posts-only deploy read a directory the build no longer emits, publishing nothing and then removing the posts it had published before. All three now agree on the one address the build emits: the graft splits a build's output between the project's subtree and the site-level blog, a project's own blog listing page is not grafted over the assembly's, and a posts-only publish that produced no posts says so and removes nothing. Retiring a project takes its posts off the blog with it, and a deploy refuses to overwrite a post another project claims.

**`selfblog post publish` records the posts it publishes.** An out-of-band post publish wrote no published-file record, leaving its posts unclaimed: nothing accounted for them, another project's publish could overwrite them, and retiring the project left them behind on the blog. The publish now updates the posts owner's claims (schema v2, site-level `blog/<post-slug>/` paths) in the same commit that carries the files, and removes the posts it claimed before and no longer produces. A build that emitted no post pages leaves the record untouched.
